paras: The whipping of Annie Miller was the public lashing of a young Black woman at or near Vanceville, Bossier Parish, Louisiana, in mid-August 1903, after she confessed to writing a threatening letter to a white planter over a Black man's name. Her confession came while that man and her father were jailed and reportedly about to be lynched; the men were released, and residents had her whipped and ordered her out of the parish.

Whit Vance, "a leading white planter" according to the New York Sun, received a letter threatening his life and making "vile" references to his wife and family, signed with the name of Peter Dozier, a Black man of Vanceville.

Dozier was arrested along with Andrew Miller and other Black men suspected as accomplices, and both New York papers reported that a lynching was planned, the Sun calling it a "quadruple lynching." Miller's daughter then confessed, when her father was also in danger, that she had written the letter and signed Dozier's name in the hope that he would be lynched; the Sun said he had "discarded" her.

According to the Sun, a meeting of the town's white and Black residents "unanimously resolved" that she be whipped, and a committee of three carried out the sentence. The St. Martinville Weekly Messenger described instead a "formal trial" by a committee of whites and Blacks in equal numbers and said she was lashed before "hundreds of persons" until she was "almost unconscious."

The Sun reported that Dozier and the other men were released, and the Messenger that the woman would not be permitted to remain in the parish. No report of action against those who whipped her appears in the coverage.

The story ran as wire copy in the New-York Tribune and the Sun on August 17 and in the Weekly Messenger on August 22; no Black-press report of it was found. Headlines such as "Negro Woman Whipped for Letter" in the Tribune and "Lie Nearly Caused Lynching" in the Sun centered her deception, and none of the reports questioned the planned lynching or the whipping. The Tribune closed by remarking that "the dove of peace once more coos" in the town.
The Sun named her Annie Miller and the Messenger Monie Miller, while the Tribune put the whipping in "the town square" and the Messenger "near Vanceville."

reader.title: Whipping of Annie Miller
bases: A crowd-appointed committee publicly whipped a Black woman after a residents' 'trial', following a threatened lynching of four jailed Black men (A1, A2, A3); no night band or whitecap organization is reported.

Three reports from different datelines and with different details (Shreveport telegram A1, New Orleans dispatch A2, longer Louisiana account A3) agree on the letter, the jailing, the daughter's confession and the public whipping.

accounts.label: Shreveport telegram
accounts.gist: Dozier, Miller and several others were jailed and a lynching was scheduled; Miller's daughter confessed to save her father and was whipped in the town square by a committee of whites and blacks.

accounts.label: New Orleans dispatch
accounts.gist: Annie Miller, jealous of Dozier, forged his name; she confessed at an open meeting of all residents, which unanimously voted the whipping, carried out by a committee of three; the four men were released.

accounts.label: Louisiana account
accounts.gist: Monie Miller confessed when her father was in the hands of an infuriated crowd; a committee equally white and Black tried her and a committee of three lashed her before hundreds until almost unconscious; she was to leave the parish.

framing.detail: Headline 'Negro Woman Whipped for Letter'; closes with 'the dove of peace once more coos' in the town.
Headline 'Lie Nearly Caused Lynching'; treats the whipping as the unanimous verdict of the community.
Calls her 'the negress' and says the letters were so vile 'as to preclude the possibility of inaction'.

conflicts.note: The Tribune gives no first name; all three describe one woman, Andrew Miller's daughter.

versions.value: an open meeting of all white and Black residents
when her father was in the hands of a crowd of infuriated men

conflicts.note: A3 then describes a separate formal trial by committee.

record_check.dossier: One woman under two names (Annie in A2, Monie in A3); also Peter Dozier, Andrew Miller and two or more other Black men jailed and threatened with lynching

She was taken in charge by a committee of whites and blacks and whipped in the town suare before a large crowd.
